setting: Digne, a small cathedral town in the mountains of Provence, 1815
keepInMind: Les Misérables is a vast novel in five volumes, set in France between 1815 and 1832. In 1815 Napoleon has fallen for good and a Bourbon king, Louis XVIII, is back on the throne. Hugo moves slowly and often stops the story to describe, explain or argue; those pauses are part of the design, and he opens not with a plot but with a long portrait of an old bishop. Let him take his time.

setting: Digne, soon after the Bishop's arrival in 1806
keepInMind: M. Myriel, once a man of society, came back from exile after the Revolution a priest, and was made Bishop of Digne almost by chance after one exchange with Napoleon. He arrived with his sister, Mademoiselle Baptistine, and their one servant, Madame Magloire.

setting: The mountain diocese of Digne
keepInMind: The Bishop has given his palace to the hospital and keeps almost none of his salary. The poor have named him Monseigneur Bienvenu, 'Monseigneur Welcome'.

setting: Digne: the Bishop at home and among his people
keepInMind: Hugo is building a portrait, not a plot. The Bishop tours his poor, roadless diocese on foot or on a donkey and teaches by example and parable rather than sermons.

setting: The Bishop's house in Digne
keepInMind: The Bishop is indulgent toward the weak and hard only on himself. A day spent on the scaffold beside a condemned man left him badly shaken by the guillotine.

setting: The Bishop's house: its rooms, garden and street door
keepInMind: The Bishop lives on almost nothing, writes late into the night, and stays alone on the ground floor after nine, when the two women go up to bed.

setting: The mountains of the diocese, in bandit country
keepInMind: The Bishop's only valuables are six silver forks and spoons and two silver candlesticks. His street door has no lock or bolt, only a latch anyone can push.

setting: A dinner at the prefect's house in Digne
keepInMind: The Bishop crossed bandit-held mountains unarmed and came back with a stolen cathedral treasure. A priest, he says, should take no precautions against his fellow man.

setting: The Bishop's household, as described in a letter by his sister
keepInMind: A rich senator laid out his comfortable atheism at dinner, and the Bishop answered with ironic praise: a fine philosophy, but one only the rich can afford.

setting: Digne and the country outside it, a little later
keepInMind: So far the Bishop has met bandits and a cynical senator with the same calm. Remember that the Revolution ruined and scattered his own family.

setting: Digne: the Bishop's politics
keepInMind: The Bishop knelt to ask a blessing of the dying conventionary G—, an old revolutionary whom Digne shunned as all but a regicide. The town's good society muttered about it afterwards.

setting: The Bishop's household and the young priests of the diocese
keepInMind: Hugo has admitted the Bishop's one fault: he was cold to Napoleon after his fall. In everything else he was just, humble and kind.

setting: Digne: the Bishop's faith
keepInMind: No ambitious young priests gather round the Bishop, because a saint offers no advancement. Hugo used the point to attack the worship of success.

setting: Digne: a last word on the Bishop's thought
keepInMind: The Bishop's faith is an overflowing love that reaches even spiders and ants. His day ends with an hour or two under the stars in his little garden, after the women have gone to bed.

setting: Digne, early October 1815, an hour before sunset
keepInMind: Book I was one long portrait of the Bishop of Digne: a man who gave away his palace, lives on almost nothing and never locks his door. Hold that portrait in mind as Book II begins.

setting: The Bishop's house, the same evening
keepInMind: A ragged traveller has been turned away by both inns, by the prison and by every door in Digne. An old lady pointed him to the low house beside the Bishop's palace: 'Knock there.'

setting: The Bishop's dining room, moments later
keepInMind: Madame Magloire was begging the Bishop to put bolts on the door against a dangerous vagabond in town when there was a heavy knock. The Bishop said, 'Come in.'

setting: The Bishop's table, the same evening
keepInMind: The traveller is Jean Valjean, a convict just released, carrying the yellow passport that shuts every door to him. The Bishop called him 'my brother', had the silver laid and the two silver candlesticks lit.

setting: The Bishop's house, after supper
keepInMind: All through supper the Bishop never said a word that could remind Valjean of what he was, and talked only of the cheese-dairies of Pontarlier.

setting: The alcove in the Bishop's house, in the middle of the night
keepInMind: To reach his alcove Valjean had to pass through the Bishop's bedroom, where he watched Madame Magloire put the silver away in the cupboard. He asked how the Bishop knew he was not an assassin; that, said the Bishop, is God's concern.

setting: Valjean's past: the galleys of Toulon, 1796 to 1815
keepInMind: Valjean, a tree-pruner of Faverolles, broke a baker's window and stole a loaf for his sister's seven starving children. Five years in the galleys became nineteen through four escape attempts.

setting: An image: a man overboard at sea
keepInMind: This short chapter steps away from the story for a prose poem. In the galleys Valjean came to judge society and Providence and to hate them, grew prodigiously strong, and became capable of cold, reasoned evil.

setting: Toulon, the day of Valjean's release, then the road through Grasse
keepInMind: Hugo's man overboard, abandoned by a ship that sails on, stands for the convict flung out by society's penal laws: 'Who shall resuscitate it?' We are still in the past, leading up to Digne.

setting: The alcove in the Bishop's house, two in the morning
keepInMind: Free but branded by his yellow passport, Valjean has been cheated of his savings and of half his wages. He has not slept in a bed for nearly twenty years, and the Bishop's silver is in the cupboard of the next room.

setting: The door of the Bishop's bedroom, moments later
keepInMind: After an hour's struggle Valjean has taken off his shoes and drawn a short pointed iron bar from his knapsack. The Bishop's door is ajar.

setting: The Bishop's garden, the next morning at sunrise
keepInMind: Valjean stopped at the bedside of the sleeping Bishop, torn between striking him and kissing his hand. Then he took the basket of silver from the cupboard and fled over the garden wall. The candlesticks stayed on the mantel.

setting: The fields outside Digne, the same day
keepInMind: Brought back by gendarmes, Valjean heard the Bishop say the silver was a gift, and was handed the candlesticks too. The Bishop told him he had promised to become an honest man ('It is your soul that I buy from you'), though Valjean remembers no promise.

setting: Paris, 1817
keepInMind: This chapter steps away from the story to paint Paris in 1817 through its fashions, gossip and politics, and it opens a new strand. We left Valjean the night after he robbed a little Savoyard of forty sous, weeping for the first time in nineteen years and kneeling at the Bishop's door.

setting: Paris, 1817: four students and their mistresses
keepInMind: Hugo's crowded panorama of 1817 ended with four young Parisians arranging 'a fine farce'.

setting: Saint-Cloud, outside Paris, a bright summer Sunday in 1817
keepInMind: The four students are led by the rich, witty, balding Tholomyès. Fantine, a foundling from Montreuil-sur-Mer, loves him with her first and only love. The girls have begged for a 'surprise' for a year, and Tholomyès has promised one.

setting: Saint-Cloud and the countryside west of Paris, the same Sunday
keepInMind: Fantine stands apart from the other three girls: blonde, beautiful, and modest even in her abandon. She would refuse Tholomyès nothing.

setting: Bombarda's, a public house on the Champs-Élysées, late afternoon
keepInMind: All day Favorite has demanded the promised surprise, and Tholomyès keeps answering, 'Patience.'

setting: Bombarda's, at dinner
keepInMind: Hugo paused to show the royalist Sunday crowd outside and to answer a police chief who called the Paris populace harmless: that despised cat, he said, can become a lion.

setting: Bombarda's, as dinner goes on
keepInMind: The table talk is loose and gay. Favorite has just told Dahlia, under her breath, that she detests Blachevelle and loves a poor young actor across the way.

setting: Bombarda's, near the end of dinner
keepInMind: Tholomyès, drunk, has held forth on everything and called Fantine a dreaming nymph who does not even hear him. The girls are still waiting for their surprise.

setting: Bombarda's, moments later
keepInMind: The four men kissed their mistresses on the brow and filed out with their fingers on their lips: the surprise has begun. 'Don't be too long,' murmured Fantine. 'We are waiting for you.'

setting: Montfermeil, a village near Paris, in the spring of 1818
keepInMind: The 'surprise' was a farewell letter: the four students had gone home to their families and respectability. Fantine laughed with the others, then wept alone, because she has a child by Tholomyès.

setting: The Thénardiers' cook-shop at Montfermeil
keepInMind: Fantine left her little daughter Cosette with an innkeeper's wife whose two happy girls she saw on a swing, and paid in advance. Once she had gone, Thénardier told his wife the money would cover a note due the next day.

setting: The Thénardiers' inn at Montfermeil, over the following years
keepInMind: Hugo has sketched the Thénardiers: she has the stuff of a brute in her, he of a blackguard. He claims to have been a sergeant at Waterloo; their daughters are Éponine and Azelma.

setting: Montreuil-sur-Mer, Fantine's native town in the north of France, 1818
keepInMind: At the inn Cosette has become the household drudge, beaten and dressed in rags, while the Thénardiers keep raising what they charge her mother. The village calls her the Lark. Book V turns to what became of Fantine.

setting: Montreuil-sur-Mer, the years after 1815
keepInMind: Fantine's native town has been transformed by Father Madeleine, a stranger who walked in one December evening in 1815 with a knapsack and a thorn stick, saved two children from a fire, and made the whole district rich with a new way of making black glass trinkets.

setting: Montreuil-sur-Mer: the mayor at home
keepInMind: Madeleine, a quiet man of about fifty, refused the Legion of Honour and the mayoralty, then gave in and became mayor in 1820. Nothing is known of where he came from.

setting: Montreuil-sur-Mer, the beginning of 1820
keepInMind: The mayor lives simply, gives in secret and is enormously strong. His supposedly mysterious room turned out to be plain, its only remarkable objects two old candlesticks that appear to be silver.

setting: Montreuil-sur-Mer, by 1821
keepInMind: When the papers announced the death of the Bishop of Digne, M. Madeleine went into mourning and said he had been a servant in the Bishop's family in his youth. He also gives money to every little Savoyard chimney-sweep who passes through.

setting: An unpaved alley of Montreuil-sur-Mer, one morning
keepInMind: Police Inspector Javert, born in a prison and devoted to authority, is the one man in the district who does not venerate the mayor. He watches Madeleine steadily, seems to have made inquiries about his past, and once muttered, 'I think I have him!'

setting: Montreuil-sur-Mer, after the accident with the cart
keepInMind: Madeleine crawled under a loaded cart and lifted it off old Fauchelevent, a man who hates him, just after Javert remarked that he had known only one man that strong: a convict at Toulon.

returning.reminder: Cosette's mother, abandoned by Tholomyès. She left her child at Montfermeil and set out for her native town to find work.

setting: The women's workroom in Madeleine's factory
keepInMind: Fantine is back in Montreuil-sur-Mer, where nobody remembers her, earning a modest living in Madeleine's factory. Nobody there knows she has a child at Montfermeil.

setting: Montreuil-sur-Mer, after Fantine's dismissal
keepInMind: A pious gossip, Madame Victurnien, went to Montfermeil, saw the child and spread the news. Fantine was dismissed in the mayor's name with fifty francs and told to leave the district; she is in debt and cannot go.

setting: Fantine's lodging, the following winter
keepInMind: The mayor knew nothing of the dismissal: the workroom superintendent acted on her own. Fantine sews soldiers' shirts for twelve sous a day, has a dry cough, and believes the mayor sent her away.

setting: A pause for commentary
keepInMind: This short chapter steps away from the story to say what Fantine's fall means. Answering Thénardier's lying letters, she sold her hair and then her two front teeth, and, hating the mayor she blames, has become a prostitute.

setting: Montreuil-sur-Mer, a snowy evening around New Year 1823
keepInMind: Hugo has called Fantine's story society buying a slave from misery, and warned that it is an error to think fate has a bottom.

setting: The police station on the square, moments later
keepInMind: An idle dandy, Bamatabois, pushed snow down Fantine's bare back; she flew at him and clawed his face. Javert seized her and dragged her off, and Bamatabois slipped away.

setting: The infirmary in M. Madeleine's house, that night
keepInMind: Javert sentenced Fantine to six months in prison. Madeleine overruled him in the name of the law, and Fantine, who had spat in his face, learned that he never knew of her dismissal. He promised to pay her debts and bring her child.

setting: The mayor's study, one morning some weeks later
keepInMind: Fantine is gravely ill in Madeleine's infirmary, and the doctor says to bring her child quickly. The Thénardiers have pocketed his money and kept Cosette, so he had Fantine sign a note ordering them to hand the child to the bearer. Javert, meanwhile, posted a letter to the Paris prefecture.

setting: Montreuil-sur-Mer, the same day
keepInMind: Javert confessed that he had denounced the mayor to Paris as the ex-convict Jean Valjean, and that he was wrong: an old man called Champmathieu, arrested near Arras, has been identified as Valjean and goes on trial at the Arras Assizes tomorrow. Madeleine refused to dismiss him.

setting: Montreuil-sur-Mer, that afternoon
keepInMind: The doctor says Fantine is losing ground fast. Madeleine commended her to Sister Simplice, a nun who has never told a lie, in a tone she noticed, and was later seen studying a road map of France and writing figures.

setting: M. Madeleine's room, that night
keepInMind: Madeleine hired a horse and light carriage for a twenty-league journey without saying where; the hirer's sums point to Arras. All night his lodger below heard him pacing, with his window open in the bitter cold.

setting: The same room, three in the morning
keepInMind: Hugo has confirmed it: M. Madeleine is Jean Valjean. All night he has argued whether to let Champmathieu go to the galleys in his place or give himself up. He burned his old convict's clothes and the forty-sou piece, but kept the Bishop's candlesticks, and decided nothing.

setting: The road from Montreuil-sur-Mer toward Arras, early morning
keepInMind: Valjean dreamed of a dead town, woke at five to find the hired carriage at his door, and went down without having made up his mind.

setting: The infirmary at Montreuil-sur-Mer, the same day
keepInMind: Valjean is pushing on toward Arras despite a wrecked wheel and bad roads, and has only just realised that he does not know when the trial begins. Fantine has been told her child is coming 'soon'.

setting: Arras, nearly eight in the evening
keepInMind: Fantine, delirious, guessed that the mayor had gone to fetch Cosette; Sister Simplice, who will not lie, said only that he had gone away, and the hope made Fantine better. Valjean, still three leagues from Arras at seven, expects to arrive too late.

setting: The Arras courthouse in the old bishop's palace, that evening
keepInMind: Valjean booked a seat on the one o'clock mail home, found the court still sitting, and, unable to get into the crowded hall, sent the President a note: M. Madeleine, Mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer.

setting: The Assize courtroom at Arras
keepInMind: Admitted to the council-chamber, Valjean fled down the corridor, stood a quarter of an hour in the dark, came back, and found himself opening the door into the courtroom.

returning.reminder: One of three former Toulon convicts who, Javert said, swore that Champmathieu is Jean Valjean.
Another of the three ex-convicts who identified Champmathieu as Jean Valjean.
The third ex-convict witness against Champmathieu.
The idle young dandy who pushed snow down Fantine's back outside the officers' café.

setting: The courtroom, as the debate draws to a close
keepInMind: The accused, an old man in a blouse, looks like Valjean as he was entering Digne. Only his identity is really proved, by Javert and the three convicts, and the prosecutor has asked for the galleys for life.

setting: The courtroom, a moment later
keepInMind: Champmathieu rambled about his life, and the three convicts swore again that he is Jean Valjean. Then a voice behind the judges called them by name, and twenty people cried out: 'M. Madeleine!'

setting: The infirmary at Montreuil-sur-Mer, at dawn
keepInMind: Valjean declared himself before the court, proved it with details only a fellow convict could know, and walked out unhindered; the prosecutor, he said, knew where to find him. Champmathieu was acquitted within the hour.

setting: Fantine's bedside, moments later
keepInMind: Sister Simplice was shocked to see that the mayor's hair had turned white overnight. Fantine woke, and her first words were 'And Cosette?' She believes he has brought her.

setting: Fantine's sickroom: what had happened during the night
keepInMind: Fantine chattered happily about Cosette while Valjean and the doctor put her off. Then, terrified, she signed to him to look behind him: Javert stood in the doorway.

setting: Fantine's sickroom, the same morning
keepInMind: After Champmathieu's acquittal a warrant was issued for the convict Jean Valjean and sent to Javert, who stands in the doorway with soldiers behind him, transfigured by a terrible joy.

setting: Montreuil-sur-Mer, the day of the arrest
keepInMind: Javert seized Valjean by the collar in front of Fantine and shouted that there was no mayor, only a convict. Learning that her child had never come, she died. Valjean whispered something in her ear, laid her out, and gave himself up.

setting: The road from Nivelles in Belgium, a May morning in 1861
keepInMind: This chapter steps away from the story to begin Hugo's long account of the battle of Waterloo, opening with his own visit to the field. We left Valjean escaped from Montreuil-sur-Mer toward Paris, and Fantine thrown into a common grave.

setting: Hougomont, a walled farm on the field of Waterloo
keepInMind: A cannonball hole in a farm gate told the narrator where he was standing: on the battlefield of Waterloo. Book I of this volume is Hugo's essay on the battle, so read it on its own terms.

setting: Waterloo, the night of 17 to 18 June 1815
keepInMind: Three thousand men died in the one enclosure of Hougomont, the first obstacle Napoleon met at Waterloo. Hugo's digression on the battle continues.

setting: The battlefield, laid out like a map
keepInMind: Hugo argues that the rain of that night lost Napoleon the battle: the wet ground delayed his artillery until half-past eleven and gave Blücher's Prussians time to come up.

setting: Waterloo, 18 June, from 11:35 in the morning
keepInMind: Picture the field as a capital A: Wellington on the high ground of Mont-Saint-Jean at the top, Napoleon below at the foot, and the whole battle a fight for the plateau.

setting: The English lines, toward four in the afternoon
keepInMind: The French took the farms of La Haie-Sainte and Papelotte. From noon to four the fighting dissolved into a melee no historian can map.

setting: Napoleon's side of the field, the night before and the morning of the battle
keepInMind: Around four o'clock Wellington pulled his line back behind the crest of the plateau, and Napoleon took it for the beginning of a retreat.

setting: Napoleon at his post on the morning of Waterloo
keepInMind: Along the crest of Mont-Saint-Jean, invisible from the French side, runs the sunken road from Ohain, a trench as much as twelve feet deep.

setting: The valley below Mont-Saint-Jean, in the afternoon
keepInMind: Sure that Wellington was retreating, Napoleon sent word to Paris that the battle was won and ordered Milhaud's cuirassiers to carry the plateau. His guide Lacoste had shaken his head at a question.

setting: The plateau of Mont-Saint-Jean
keepInMind: The cuirassiers' charge plunged into the hidden road of Ohain until the ravine was filled with men and horses. Hugo says Napoleon could not have won: 'He embarrassed God.'

setting: The heights toward Frischemont, about five o'clock
keepInMind: The English squares held for two hours against the surviving cuirassiers. At five Wellington murmured, 'Blücher, or night!' as a line of bayonets gleamed in the distance.

setting: The field at nightfall
keepInMind: The bayonets were Bülow's Prussians, well guided by a shepherd, while Napoleon had been told the distant 'cloud' was his own Marshal Grouchy.

setting: The French lines, as the army breaks
keepInMind: The Imperial Guard went into the fight shouting 'Vive l'Empereur!' and was cut down. Marshal Ney sought death everywhere and could not find it.

setting: The valley at the foot of Mont-Saint-Jean, toward nine at night
keepInMind: The French army has collapsed on every side and the Prussians are slaughtering the fugitives. Napoleon was last seen on foot, turning back alone toward the field.

setting: The last square of the Guard, nine in the evening
keepInMind: Called on to surrender, Cambronne, commanding the last square, answered with a single obscene word.

setting: After the battle: Hugo's verdict
keepInMind: This chapter steps back from the fighting to weigh the commanders. The Guard is dead, and Hugo has named Cambronne, not any general, the true victor of Waterloo.

setting: Waterloo considered as politics
keepInMind: This chapter steps away to judge what Waterloo meant. Hugo gave the glory to the English soldier rather than to Wellington, and called the day more massacre than battle.

setting: France and Europe after 1815
keepInMind: Hugo called Waterloo a counter-revolutionary victory of Europe's kings over France and the Revolution, which nonetheless forced the returning Bourbons to grant a charter.

setting: The battlefield of Waterloo, the night of 18 June 1815
keepInMind: Hugo has sketched the Restoration that followed, with Napoleon caged on Saint Helena. Now he goes back to the field itself after the last shot, under a full moon.

setting: Paris and Toulon, in 1823
keepInMind: The story comes back from Waterloo to where it left off. Valjean escaped from Montreuil-sur-Mer toward Paris after slipping back to take the Bishop's candlesticks, and Fantine was buried in a common pit.

returning.reminder: The ex-convict who was M. Madeleine, mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer. He gave himself up to save Champmathieu, was arrested at Fantine's deathbed, and broke out of the town jail.

setting: Montfermeil, at about the same time in 1823
keepInMind: Valjean was retaken in Paris just as he boarded a coach for Montfermeil, tried for robbing little Gervais, and sent back to Toulon for life as number 9,430. A large sum he withdrew from Laffitte's bank during his days of freedom has never been found.

setting: Toulon harbour, late October 1823
keepInMind: At Montfermeil an ex-convict road-mender, Boulatruelle, let slip that he saw a man he knew from the galleys bury a small chest in the forest. He has been digging for it ever since.

setting: Montfermeil, Christmas Eve 1823
keepInMind: The Toulon paper has reported convict number 9,430, Jean Valjean, drowned after rescuing a sailor from the rigging of the Orion; the body was not found. The story now goes back to the Thénardiers' inn.

returning.reminder: Fantine's little daughter, left at the Thénardiers' inn as a toddler and kept there as their drudge, 'the Lark'.
The innkeeper's huge, violent wife, who beats Cosette and spoils her own two daughters.
The Montfermeil innkeeper who bled Fantine with lying letters. A prowler named Thénardier also robbed a wounded officer on the field of Waterloo.
The Thénardiers' elder daughter, who used to swing in front of the inn.

setting: The Thénardiers' inn, the same evening
keepInMind: Kept on as a servant since Fantine's money stopped, Cosette sits knitting under the kitchen table while carters drink in the public room. She dreads being sent to the forest spring after dark.

setting: The inn's public room, Christmas Eve
keepInMind: Hugo has drawn the Thénardiers in full: she rules by blows, he by cunning. He tells of having saved a wounded general at Waterloo.

setting: Boulanger Alley, outside the inn, the same evening
keepInMind: Madame Thénardier has sent Cosette, eight years old and bruised from a blow, to fetch water from the spring in the forest, with a bucket bigger than she is and a fifteen-sou piece to buy bread.

setting: The road out of Montfermeil toward the forest spring, that night
keepInMind: Cosette stood spellbound before a splendid doll in the toy stall opposite the inn until Madame Thénardier's shout sent her running.

setting: The Boulevard de l'Hôpital in Paris, the afternoon of Christmas Day 1823
keepInMind: At the spring Cosette lost her fifteen-sou piece in the water without knowing it. Staggering home under the bucket, she cried 'O my God!', and a man's hand silently took the weight. She was not afraid.

setting: The dark road back to Montfermeil, the same night
keepInMind: The stranger is a white-haired man in a threadbare yellow coat who came out from Paris that afternoon, avoiding the police, and checked a particular clearing in the forest before he came upon Cosette.

setting: The Thénardiers' door, that night
keepInMind: Cosette told the stranger she is eight, works all day for Madame Thénardier and has no mother that she knows of; her name gave him a visible shock. He means to lodge at the inn, and he gave back the bucket at the door so that she would not be beaten.

setting: The inn's public room, two hours before dawn
keepInMind: Taken for a beggar, the stranger saved Cosette from a whipping over the lost coin, bought her the splendid doll, which she named Catherine, and in the night slipped a gold louis into her wooden shoe on the hearth.

setting: The inn, just after the stranger and Cosette have left
keepInMind: Thénardier pretended to adore Cosette, then sold her to the stranger for fifteen hundred francs. She walked out of Montfermeil at daybreak in new mourning clothes, holding her doll, on the road toward Livry.

setting: The forest beyond Montfermeil, and the road to Paris
keepInMind: Thénardier ran after the pair to squeeze out more money. The stranger produced a note signed by Fantine ordering Cosette handed to the bearer, then walked off into the woods with the child and stared Thénardier down until he gave up.

setting: The Boulevard de l'Hôpital, at the bleak southern edge of Paris
keepInMind: Jean Valjean is alive: he swam away from the Orion, crossed France in secret, and took Cosette from the Thénardiers. He is carrying her, asleep, toward the Boulevard de l'Hôpital. This chapter steps away to describe the house he is heading for.

setting: The Gorbeau house, the same night
keepInMind: The Gorbeau house is a dilapidated, half-empty building at the desolate edge of Paris, between the Salpêtrière and the city wall.

setting: The attic in the Gorbeau house, the next morning at daybreak
keepInMind: Valjean carried the sleeping Cosette into an attic he had prepared. She woke expecting to be set to work, and he told her to play.

setting: The Gorbeau house, over the following weeks
keepInMind: Valjean, who has never loved anyone, loves Cosette like a father, and she, who has never been loved, calls him 'father'. He teaches her to read and talks to her of her mother.

setting: Near Saint-Médard's church and the Gorbeau house, late winter 1824
keepInMind: Valjean goes out only after dark and is known locally as 'the beggar who gives alms'. The nosy old woman who keeps the house saw him take a thousand-franc note from his coat lining, and found wigs in his pockets.

setting: The streets of Paris, a moonlit night in March 1824
keepInMind: Valjean thought he glimpsed Javert's face under a beggar's rags. Then a tall new lodger listened at his door by night, and at dawn Valjean recognised Javert's back. At dark he left with Cosette.

setting: The Rue des Postes, toward eleven that night
keepInMind: From a doorway Valjean watched four men confer under the moon, and recognised Javert at their head.

setting: Beyond the Pont d'Austerlitz, the same night
keepInMind: Valjean crossed the Pont d'Austerlitz in the shadow of a cart, but looking back he saw four shadows stepping onto the bridge.

setting: The Petit-Picpus quarter: the corner of the Rue Polonceau and the Rue Droit-Mur
keepInMind: Valjean is trapped between a blind alley and a sentinel guarding the only way out, with Javert's squad behind him. Hugo paused to describe this lost quarter from an old map of 1727.

setting: The Rue Polonceau, moments later
keepInMind: Hidden in a niche of the wall, Valjean has found the drainpipe too weak to climb, the carriage gate immovable, and the great door a wooden sham over solid stone.

setting: A vast garden behind the wall
keepInMind: Valjean cut down a street lantern's rope, tied Cosette to it, climbed the wall and hauled her up, and dropped with her into a garden as Javert ordered the blind alley searched.

setting: The garden, between one and two in the morning
keepInMind: Hiding in a ruined shed, Valjean and Cosette heard women's voices singing a hymn in the dark building above the garden, and knelt.

setting: The ruined shed, later that night
keepInMind: Looking for shelter, Valjean saw through a lit window a shrouded form lying face down with its arms outstretched and something like a rope round its neck, and fled in terror. He has a fever; Cosette is asleep.

setting: The garden, before dawn
keepInMind: A limping man with a bell is moving about the melon beds. Cosette's hands are icy and she will not wake: Valjean must get her to a bed by a fire within a quarter of an hour.

setting: The pursuit retold from Javert's side, from December 1823
keepInMind: The man with the bell is old Fauchelevent, whom Valjean once lifted from under a cart and placed here as gardener; he still calls him Father Madeleine and has taken them into his hut. The house is the convent of the Petit-Picpus.

setting: No. 62 Rue Petit-Picpus, half a century ago
keepInMind: Javert picked up Valjean's trail from a report of a child taken from Montfermeil and from 'the beggar who gives alms', but delayed the arrest and lost him at the wall. This chapter steps away from the story to take the reader inside the convent.

setting: The convent of the Petit-Picpus, 1824
keepInMind: This chapter steps away from the story to describe the rule of the house. The convent behind the wall belongs to the Bernardines of the Perpetual Adoration: men are refused, and a nun may be heard through the parlour grating but not seen.

setting: Inside the Petit-Picpus convent: novices and pupils
keepInMind: Hugo's tour of the convent continues, away from the story. The nuns live by fasts, silence, night offices and the twelve-hour 'reparation' lying prostrate with a rope round the neck, which may remind you of the figure Valjean glimpsed through the window.

setting: The convent's boarding-school
keepInMind: Still Hugo's portrait of the convent. A boarding-school of well-born girls is attached to it; they see even their mothers only through the parlour bars.

setting: The convent school: refectory, garden and dormitories
keepInMind: Hugo is gathering the childhood that fills the gloomy cloister: recreation hours in the garden and the pupils' sayings, which he says he collected there.

setting: The enclosure of the Petit-Picpus: its three houses
keepInMind: These convent chapters are anecdotes and description and do not move the plot: silent meals, forbidden reading, a mad nun, a flute heard from the Rue Droit-Mur.

setting: The Petit-Picpus, 1819 to 1825: its people
keepInMind: The enclosure holds the Great Convent of the nuns, the boarding-school, and the Little Convent of aged nuns from orders the Revolution destroyed, all divided by a church built so that no outsider can see a face.

setting: The convent's ground plan
keepInMind: Note the prioress, Mother Innocente, and the code of bells by which this silent house speaks. Apart from the archbishop and the gardener, the pupils see only two men, both carefully chosen.

setting: The Little Convent
keepInMind: Hugo has mapped the enclosure: a sunken garden radiating from a central fir, its walls far higher inside than out, bounded by the Rue Polonceau and the Rue Droit-Mur, the streets Valjean fled through.

setting: Other convent parlours, and the origins of the order
keepInMind: The digression goes on. The last chapter was a comic tale of a hundred-year-old nun and the secret treasure she kept locked away.

setting: The Petit-Picpus from the Restoration onward
keepInMind: Hugo has traced how the Perpetual Adoration was founded. Valjean and Cosette are still in the gardener's hut, where the story left them.

setting: Hugo's 'Parenthesis': the convent as an idea
keepInMind: Book VII is a 'Parenthesis': these chapters step away from the story entirely to reflect on convents and prayer. Hugo has stated his stance: respect without belief, and vigilance against a past that disguises itself as the future.

setting: The Parenthesis: the convent judged by history
keepInMind: Hugo called this book a drama whose chief personage is the Infinite, and the convent one of man's instruments for reaching toward it, hideous on one side and sublime on the other.

setting: The Parenthesis: respecting the past
keepInMind: Hugo condemned monasticism by history and reason, citing the in pace dungeon he saw for himself at the Abbey of Villers.

setting: The Parenthesis: the convent in principle
keepInMind: Hugo will respect the past only on condition that it consents to be dead, and fights it where it insists on living, while refusing to exaggerate.

setting: The Parenthesis: prayer
keepInMind: In principle, Hugo granted, the convent rests on the right of association and practises equality: its members share the same cell and bread and elect those they obey. He ended by asking what these kneeling people are doing.

setting: The Parenthesis: the goodness of prayer
keepInMind: They pray. Hugo described prayer as the contact of two infinities, one above us and one within, and called for crushing fanaticism while venerating the infinite.

setting: The Parenthesis: blaming with care
keepInMind: All sincere prayer is good, Hugo says; denying the infinite leads to nihilism, and faith and love are the two motors of progress.

setting: The Parenthesis: faith and law
keepInMind: The convent, Hugo says, is a contradiction, supreme egoism yielding supreme self-sacrifice. One may frown at it, but never sneer. This is the last chapter of the Parenthesis.

setting: Fauchelevent's hut in the convent garden, the morning after Valjean came over the wall
keepInMind: The story resumes after nineteen chapters on the convent. Valjean and Cosette are hiding with the gardener, who promised to ask no questions; outside, Javert's men are watching the streets.

returning.reminder: The ex-convict who was M. Madeleine. Reported drowned at Toulon, he took Cosette from the Thénardiers and escaped Javert by climbing into the convent garden.
Fantine's daughter, about eight, rescued from the Thénardiers; she calls Valjean 'father'.
The old carter whom M. Madeleine pulled from under his cart and found a post as gardener in a Paris convent. He wears a bell so the nuns can avoid him.

setting: The prioress's parlour, the same day
keepInMind: A nun has just died, and the pupils would discover any strange man in the garden: to stay, Valjean must first get out and come back in by the door as a newcomer. Fauchelevent has been summoned to the prioress.

returning.reminder: The prioress of the Petit-Picpus, a learned and merry nun; only she may deal with outsiders.

setting: The parlour, a quarter of an hour later
keepInMind: Fauchelevent asked the prioress to take on his 'brother', a fine gardener, and a little girl to be raised in the house. She answered only by asking whether he could get a stout iron bar to serve as a lever by evening.

setting: Fauchelevent's hut, soon afterwards
keepInMind: The dead nun, Mother Crucifixion, asked to be buried in her own coffin under the chapel altar, which the law forbids. Fauchelevent must help in secret and fill the empty official coffin with earth; then he may bring his brother and the child.

setting: The Boulevard du Maine and the Vaugirard cemetery, the next afternoon
keepInMind: Valjean's plan: he will be nailed into the empty official coffin and carried to Vaugirard, where Fauchelevent will get the drunken gravedigger, Father Mestienne, out of the way and dig him up.

setting: Inside the coffin, the same afternoon
keepInMind: Mestienne is dead. The new gravedigger, Gribier, never drinks, and the hearse has stopped beside an open grave.

setting: Above the grave, the same moments
keepInMind: Lowered into the grave, Valjean heard the prayers and the footsteps going away, then earth falling on the lid. One of his air holes was stopped up, and he lost consciousness.

setting: The Rue Petit-Picpus, an hour later, after dark
keepInMind: Fauchelevent stole Gribier's card and sent him running home for it, opened the coffin, and found Valjean alive. They buried the empty coffin and left the cemetery with the card.

setting: The convent, after Valjean's admission
keepInMind: Valjean has been taken in as the gardener's brother under the name Ultime Fauchelevent, and Cosette as a charity pupil, because the prioress judged she would grow up plain.

setting: Paris: the street child
keepInMind: A new volume begins, and this chapter steps away from the story to portray the gamin, the Paris street boy; the whole of Book I is an essay on him. We left Valjean gardening in the convent and Cosette growing up there over many years.

setting: Paris: the gamin's ways
keepInMind: Still Hugo's portrait of the Paris street boy: ragged, homeless and foul-mouthed, yet innocent at heart. 'It is my little one,' says the city.

setting: Paris: the gamin at the theatre
keepInMind: The gamin has his own trades, his own scrap-copper coinage and a quick, cynical wit.

setting: Paris: the gamin and the lounger
keepInMind: At night the gamin becomes the irreverent titi of the theatre gallery, and nothing frightens or astonishes him.

setting: The banlieue: the fringe of Paris beyond the barriers
keepInMind: Hugo's essay on the gamin continues. He set the street boy and the idle lounger side by side as the two extremes of Paris.

setting: Paris and its abandoned children
keepInMind: The banlieue, the melancholy half-wild fringe of the city, is the whole world to the gamin; nothing exists for him two leagues beyond the barriers.

setting: Paris: the gamins as a caste
keepInMind: Hundreds of children are abandoned in Paris every year, yet the city's air, Hugo says, keeps its street boys inwardly intact. Under the old monarchy such children were sent to the galleys.

setting: Paris: the gamin in summer, on the river and in the streets
keepInMind: The gamins form almost a caste, ranked by scars, left-handedness and, above all, by attending executions.

setting: The gamin and the Gallic spirit
keepInMind: The gamin swims naked in the Seine, draws pears on walls, hates priests and knows every policeman in Paris by sight.

setting: Paris as the sum of history
keepInMind: Gaminerie, Hugo says, is a shade of the old Gallic spirit, and the street boy can turn from scapegrace to hero in a moment, like the drummer-boy Barra.

setting: Paris and the world
keepInMind: Since the gamin expresses Paris, Hugo has widened his essay into a portrait of the city itself: Athens, Rome and Jerusalem in one.

setting: The faubourgs of Paris and their people
keepInMind: Paris sets the fashion and the law for the world, Hugo says, and its secret is daring.

setting: The Boulevard du Temple, Paris, eight or nine years after the events of Volume II
keepInMind: Hugo's essay ended with the Paris populace as a grown-up gamin, barefoot and unlettered, who could be made sublime by education. The story now resumes years later; we left Valjean and Cosette inside the convent.

setting: The Marais, Paris, around 1831
keepInMind: The street boy is Little Gavroche, unloved son of the destitute Jondrettes, who live in the old Gorbeau house where Valjean and Cosette once hid. Their neighbour there is a very poor young man called M. Marius, and Hugo has promised to explain who he is.

setting: M. Gillenormand's house in the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire
keepInMind: M. Gillenormand is over ninety, loud, hale and quick with his cane: a bourgeois relic of the eighteenth century, with an unmarried daughter past fifty whom he scolds like a child.

setting: M. Gillenormand's youth and opinions
keepInMind: Gillenormand dresses like a dandy of the Directory, has had two wives, and holds the French Revolution to be a heap of blackguards.

setting: M. Gillenormand's prides and hopes
keepInMind: He cherishes memories of the opera beauties of his youth and despises the politicians of the day. His godfather named him Luc-Esprit.

setting: M. Gillenormand's household
keepInMind: He adores the Bourbons, has a horror of 1789, and means to live to a hundred.

setting: M. Gillenormand's family
keepInMind: He renames every manservant after his province and calls every maid Nicolette, including one called Magnon.

setting: Gillenormand's habits, from the early Restoration on
keepInMind: Magnon sent the old man two baby boys, naming him as father; flattered, he denied it but pays for both. Of his two daughters, the younger married for love a soldier of the Empire, made colonel at Waterloo, whom Gillenormand calls the disgrace of his family, and she died.

setting: The Gillenormand household
keepInMind: Gillenormand lived near Saint-Sulpice during the early Restoration and moved to the Marais only after eighty. His door stays shut all day; he receives only after dinner at five.

setting: The Rue Servandoni and an ultra-royalist salon, about 1817
keepInMind: Living with Gillenormand are his elder daughter, a prude and bigot who keeps house for him, and a small boy, his grandson, whom he bullies and idolises.

setting: Vernon, a little town on the Seine, in the same years
keepInMind: In Madame de T.'s salon the old man's handsome little grandson was pitied as 'poor child', because his father was 'a brigand of the Loire': Gillenormand's despised son-in-law.

setting: Madame de T.'s salon, through Marius's boyhood
keepInMind: The scarred old soldier growing flowers at Vernon is Colonel Georges Pontmercy, made baron at Waterloo, and the boy is his son Marius. Gillenormand took Marius from him on pain of disinheritance; the colonel watches him secretly at mass, and Marius has been taught to think of him with shame.

setting: Paris and Vernon, 1827
keepInMind: Raised in Madame de T.'s fossilised salon, Marius has grown into a grave, proud, fanatical young royalist who does not much love his grandfather and is gloomy about his father. He is now a law student.

setting: Saint-Sulpice, one Sunday
keepInMind: Marius reached Vernon too late: his father died rising to meet him. Marius kept the colonel's note, which leaves him the title of baron and asks him to do all the good he can to a sergeant named Thénardier who saved his life at Waterloo. You saw that night on the battlefield: the 'rescue' was a robbery. Within three days Marius had forgotten his father.

setting: Paris, after three days away
keepInMind: Old M. Mabeuf, a churchwarden at Saint-Sulpice, told Marius how a poor father came secretly for years to gaze at the son he was forbidden to see: Colonel Pontmercy. Marius then asked his grandfather for three days' leave, which the old man took for a love affair.

setting: The Gillenormand house, some time later
keepInMind: Marius has read the history of the Republic and the Empire, come to adore his father and Napoleon, had cards engraved 'Le Baron Marius Pontmercy', looked in vain for Thénardier at Montfermeil, and wears something on a black ribbon round his neck.

returning.reminder: Lieutenant Théodule, Mademoiselle Gillenormand's favourite: a lancer grand-nephew of the old man.

setting: Paris, after Théodule's trip to Vernon
keepInMind: Sent by the aunt to spy on Marius, Théodule found that the 'lass' was a grave: Marius sobbing on the grave of Colonel Baron Pontmercy at Vernon.

setting: The Latin Quarter of Paris, about 1828
keepInMind: Marius shouted 'Down with the Bourbons!' at his grandfather and was turned out with thirty francs; the medallion holding his father's note was lost on the stairs. This chapter pauses the story to introduce a group of young republicans.

setting: Outside the Café Musain, one afternoon
keepInMind: The Friends of the A.B.C. are a small secret society of republican students meeting at the Café Musain: Enjolras the chief, Combeferre, Courfeyrac, Bossuet (also called Laigle), Joly, Bahorel, Prouvaire, Feuilly, and the sceptic Grantaire, who believes only in Enjolras.

setting: The Latin Quarter, the days that follow
keepInMind: Laigle answered to Marius's name at a law-school roll-call and was struck off himself. Courfeyrac took the homeless Marius to lodge beside him at the hôtel de la Porte-Saint-Jacques.

setting: The back room of the Café Musain, a winter evening
keepInMind: Marius calls himself a 'democrat-Bonapartist'. The Friends' irreverent talk has begun to unsettle the convictions he had just won, and none of them says 'the Emperor'.

setting: The back room of the Café Musain, the same evening
keepInMind: The talk has run from Grantaire's drunken scorn for every nation to Courfeyrac throwing a copy of the Charter into the fire. Marius has mostly listened.
